Incorporating SLOOS alongside the November 2, 2022 FOMC statement shifts the tone more negative. The policy stance is already restrictive (75bp hike to 3.75–4.00%, QT ongoing), and SLOOS shows the bank credit channel tightening and demand cooling, amplifying the contractionary impulse beyond policy rates alone.

SLOOS cross-check highlights:
- Broad tightening in supply of credit: banks reported tighter standards for C&I loans (including foreign banks) and across CRE segments (construction/land development, nonfarm nonresidential, multifamily). Consumer credit also tightened, notably credit cards and multiple mortgage categories; auto standards were largely unchanged.
- Weaker loan demand: firms of all sizes reported weaker C&I demand; consumer demand weaker for credit cards and auto, with some offset from stronger HELOC demand.
- Underwriting selectivity increased: banks less likely to approve lower FICO (620/680) and more likely at higher FICO (720), consistent with tighter risk appetite.
- Drivers and outlook: economic outlook cited as a reason for tightening, and banks’ recession likelihood assessments rose.

These SLOOS signals validate the FOMC’s emphasis on “cumulative tightening” and policy lags, but they also indicate financial conditions are biting harder, increasing downside growth risks even as inflation remains elevated. Net effect: a more negative read than the FSR-only baseline.
